name: DNA to Protein Translation Calculator
seoTitle: DNA to Protein Translation Calculator — Formula & Results
seoDesc: Translation reads a nucleotide sequence three bases at a time and writes the amino acids it encodes. Free dna to protein translation calculator: enter your va
summary:
Translation reads a nucleotide sequence three bases at a time and writes the amino acids it encodes. It returns coding length, amino acids in the longest frame, stop codons in frame 1 and mass of the frame-1 protein, and the panel shows all of them at once.

Because the reading frame is not marked in the sequence, the same DNA gives three completely different proteins — this calculator shows all six frames, three from each strand, which is how a real open reading frame is found. Every result is derived from the boxes you fill in, so changing one input updates the whole panel at once. Units are stated on every box and in every result, so a figure copied out of a protocol, a datasheet or a chart can be entered without converting it first.

sections.title: The formula behind the DNA to Protein Translation
sections.html:
Each codon of three bases maps to one amino acid; the standard genetic code is used

sections.title: How do I use the DNA to Protein Translation?
sections.html:
The form asks only for what the formula needs — nothing is optional decoration.

  1. Enter the values you already have. Every box accepts a decimal point and a minus sign; thousands separators are ignored.
  2. The grey boxes are results: they are worked out from your inputs and cannot be typed into.
  3. Press Calculate. The results fill in together, and from then on they follow every edit you make — there is no page to reload and nothing to submit.

sections.title: A worked example
sections.html: The arithmetic is the page's own: change one box and the result moves by the amount the formula implies, which is the quickest way to convince yourself the tool is honest.

sections.title: What does the result mean?
sections.html:
A raw figure only means something next to the bands it is normally judged against. Here is the scale that goes with this one:

How to read the result
ResultBandWhat it means
ATGStartmethionine, and the usual start of an ORF
TAA, TAG, TGAStopdo not encode an amino acid
3 frames per strandSix in totalonly one is normally the real gene

  • The reverse strand is read as its reverse complement, which is why a gene can be on either strand of a chromosome.

  • A long open reading frame — a hundred codons or more with no stop — is the strongest sequence-level evidence that a region is protein-coding.

  • The mass uses average residue masses, so it matches what a mass spectrometer reports rather than the monoisotopic mass.

sections.title: What are the common mistakes?
sections.html:
The arithmetic is simple; the inputs are where things go wrong. The usual culprits:

  • Translating a sequence that still contains introns and wondering why there are stops every few codons.
  • Assuming frame 1 is the gene: roughly half of human genes are on the reverse strand.
  • Pasting an alignment with gaps, which shifts every downstream codon.

faq.q: How do I find the reading frame of a gene?
faq.a: Translate all six frames and look for the long open reading frame that starts with ATG and ends with a stop codon.

faq.q: Why does my translation have so many stops?
faq.a: Almost always the wrong frame, or a genomic sequence where a cDNA was expected.

faq.q: What does the DNA to Protein Translation actually calculate?
faq.a: It returns coding length, amino acids in the longest frame, stop codons in frame 1 and mass of the frame-1 protein. Each one is derived by the formula on this page, so you can check any figure by hand.

faq.q: Do I have to fill in every box?
faq.a: Fill in the ones you know. The result boxes are computed from them, so you never enter a value the formula can derive — and if you change an input, every result updates with it.

faq.q: Why is the answer different from the one in my protocol?
faq.a: Nearly always a unit or a rounding difference. This calculator works in the units printed next to each box, keeps full precision internally and only rounds for display, so recomputing from the rounded numbers on screen can differ in the last digit.

faq.q: Can I use it with the numbers straight from a datasheet?
faq.a: Yes. Every box states its unit, and nothing is converted behind your back, so a figure copied from a datasheet, a kit insert or a protocol goes in as printed.
